issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Exposed to Others: I feel that others can see what happened to me just by looking at me
issues.explanation: The negative appraisal items 'others can see what happened to me' and 'ashamed of what happened to my body' imply a trauma with visible bodily violation or injury, most classically interpersonal/sexual trauma, and are hard to reconcile with a generic man-made disaster trauma in the absence of any corroborating memory or trigger content about bodily injury or disfigurement.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Body Shame: I feel ashamed of what happened to my body
issues.explanation: 'Avoid Being Touched' is specifically linked to bodily violation/contact-based trauma and fits poorly with the rest of the profile for man-made disaster. The threat items center on environmental danger and escape planning, creating a cross-node mismatch with this touch-avoidance strategy.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Body Shame: I feel ashamed of what happened to my body
issues.explanation: These items imply a trauma with prominent bodily violation or physical injury consequences. For a man-made disaster trauma, this specific body-focused pattern is not impossible, but in the absence of any supporting memory or trigger content and alongside the other items emphasizing generalized danger, it stands out as a hard-to-explain shift toward an assault/injury formulation.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Being Touched: Any form of physical contact with others
issues.explanation: Within the current profile, avoidance of touch and bodily stress appears organized around bodily harm/shame, but the threat items are about environmental danger, escape planning, and unfamiliar places. That makes the strategy set only partially connected to the expressed threat/appraisal pattern.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Failed Role: I have failed in my most important role in life
issues.explanation: The profile is otherwise centered on persistent danger, vigilance, scanning, escape planning, and avoidance of unfamiliar places, which coheres with threat-focused beliefs after a man-made disaster. 'Failed Role' introduces a distinct self-evaluative theme that is not supported by the rest of the selected items and is hard to reconcile with this otherwise purely danger/safety formulation. Given the active formulation emphasizes Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies and Maladaptive Strategies → Threat, a danger-based appraisal would better fit the linked hypervigilance and checking strategies than a role-failure appraisal.

vignette:
Priya enters a room the way a sapper enters a minefield. At thirty-two, the city council member, once known for her easy confidence, now moves with a rigid, calculated caution. Her eyes are never still, constantly scanning the space not for constituents or colleagues, but for structural weaknesses and, most importantly, for ways out. This has been her reality for the eight months since the collapse of the Northwood Community Center, a project she had championed and celebrated right up until the moment its roof gave way. The trauma was not the fall itself, but the hours that followed: the suffocating darkness, the taste of plaster dust, the weight on her chest that made every breath a desperate, burning struggle, and the disorienting screams from unseen victims.

In the months that followed, the initial relief of survival curdled into a pervasive, gnawing dread. Priya had come to believe that the world was fundamentally a dangerous place, and that the safety she had once taken for granted was a fragile illusion. Her mind now operates on the principle that she must be on guard at all times, because you never know what can happen next. This conviction dictates the shape of her days. At City Hall, a building she once navigated with effortless familiarity, she now finds herself unable to settle into a meeting until she has mentally mapped at least two escape routes. During public forums, she scans the faces in the crowd, her focus not on the content of their questions but on a frantic search for anyone who looks agitated or unpredictable, anyone she deems a potential source of danger.

Her professional life, once her pride, has become a landscape of triggers. She has started declining invitations to ribbon-cuttings and site visits if they are in unfamiliar locations, citing scheduling conflicts when the truth is she cannot bear the anxiety of entering a space whose potential hazards she hasn't had time to assess. The avoidance extends beyond her work. She used to be an avid runner, but now avoids any physical exertion that makes her heart pound and her breathing quicken; the sensation is too similar to the memory of fighting for air in the rubble. Situations that put her body under any kind of stress feel like a direct threat, a prelude to being trapped again.

Night is the hardest. As darkness falls, so does a heavier blanket of fear, a certainty that threats are more potent when they are unseen. Priya finds it almost impossible to feel safe in her own home after sundown, often staying up late, moving from window to window, checking locks, listening for any sound that is out of place. Her world has shrunk to a small collection of "safe" zones: her office, her apartment, and the two blocks in between. Everything outside this perimeter feels charged with a malevolent uncertainty.

The decision to seek therapy came after a particularly humiliating incident last week. During a routine zoning committee meeting held in the basement of a local church—an unfamiliar venue—the sense of being underground, coupled with the lack of large windows, became overwhelming. She felt the walls closing in, the air growing thick and heavy. Convinced the ceiling was about to fail, she abruptly stood up mid-presentation and fled the room, leaving her colleagues stunned. The professional fallout was manageable, but the internal collapse was not. Priya arrived at her first session terrified that the capable, confident woman who had cut the ribbon at the community center that day was gone forever, buried under the weight of her own vigilance. Her hope, she stated quietly, is to one day walk into a room and simply be there, without first planning her escape.
